subject: mathematics
question_text: If x and y are natural numbers with x ≠ y, show by mathematical induction that xⁿ − yⁿ is divisible by x − y, ∀ n ∈ N.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.29, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 8(ii). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. The condition x ≠ y is stated in the answer itself, in the opening step, because it is what makes x − y a non-zero divisor. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — what is held fixed, and the add-and-subtract move that makes the third step work.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks. Two things go here: x and y are fixed with x ≠ y, and divisibility is written as an equation.
lines: x, y ∈ N and x ≠ y, so x − y ≠ 0.
The induction is on n only.

recall.must_convey: That x and y are fixed natural numbers with x ≠ y so x − y is not zero, and that divisibility is written as x to the n minus y to the n equals (x − y) times an integer q.
accept: x and y are fixed and not equal so x minus y is non zero and we write the expression as x minus y times q
divisible by x minus y means it equals x minus y times some integer
hold x and y fixed and induct on n only
x minus y into q ga rastam q integer
reject: let s of n be the statement
it is divisible by x minus y

steps.why: Two conditions do real work here. x ≠ y keeps x − y from being zero, and writing the claim as = (x − y)q is what lets Step 3 substitute the assumption.
common_mistakes: Leaving the statement in words, so Step 3 has nothing to use.
Forgetting to say q is an integer, which is the whole content of divisibility.
Not saying why x ≠ y matters, so x − y could be zero.
steps.memory_tip: Two lines before any proof: x ≠ y makes x − y non-zero, and divisibility becomes = (x − y)q.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. At n = 1 the expression IS x − y, so write it as (x − y) times 1 rather than just saying it is obvious.
lines: so x − y is divisible by x − y.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the expression is x − y, which is (x − y) times 1, so it is divisible by x − y.
accept: at n equals one it is x minus y which is x minus y times one
the first case is x minus y itself so it is divisible with q equal to one
put n equals one and you get x minus y
n equals one ki x minus y vasthundi q one

steps.why: The base case looks trivial, but the examiner wants the value of q named. Writing x − y = (x − y)(1) shows the integer is 1.
common_mistakes: Writing 'obvious' instead of showing x − y = (x − y)(1).
Checking n = 2 first and never doing n = 1.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1 the expression is x − y itself, so q = 1. Say the value of q.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for ONE value k, with x and y unchanged, and number the line (1).
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true for some k in N — x to the k minus y to the k equals (x − y)q with q an integer — and the line is numbered (1).
accept: assume x to the k minus y to the k is x minus y times q
suppose s of k holds with the same x and y and call it equation one
take it as true for one value k and number the line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k
then I assume s of k

steps.why: Only n changes to k. Step 3 will need this exact line to replace xᵏ − yᵏ, so it has to be written and numbered.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Replace n by k and keep x, y and q as they are. Number the line (1).

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Add and subtract x·yᵏ — that single move splits the expression into a piece with xᵏ − yᵏ and a piece with x − y.
lines: which is divisible by x − y, since
So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That x·yᵏ is added and subtracted, giving x(xᵏ − yᵏ) + yᵏ(x − y); the assumption replaces the first bracket, and (x − y) comes out as a common factor leaving the integer xq + yᵏ.
accept: add and subtract x times y to the k so it splits into x into x to the k minus y to the k plus y to the k into x minus y
substitute the assumption in the first bracket and take x minus y out as a common factor
what is left inside is x q plus y to the k which is an integer
x into y power k add and subtract chesi x minus y common teestam
reject: I show s of k plus one
heard_as: x times y to the k
x q plus y to the k

steps.why: Adding and subtracting x·yᵏ changes nothing but makes two groups appear: one containing xᵏ − yᵏ, which the assumption covers, and one containing x − y outright. Both then share the factor x − y.
common_mistakes: Writing xᵏ⁺¹ as xᵏ + x instead of x × xᵏ.
Substituting (1) straight into x·xᵏ − y·yᵏ, where no xᵏ − yᵏ has appeared yet.
Stopping at (x − y)(…) without saying the bracket is an integer, which is what divisibility requires.
steps.memory_tip: Add and subtract x·yᵏ. One group becomes x(xᵏ − yᵏ), the other becomes yᵏ(x − y).

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction xⁿ − yⁿ is divisible by x − y for every natural number n.
accept: since the first case is true and each case gives the next by p m i it is true for all n
hence by the principle of mathematical induction x to the n minus y to the n is divisible by x minus y for every natural number
base case plus inductive step gives it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni n ki true

steps.why: The two proved statements are about n = 1 and about a step. Only the principle turns them into every n, for the fixed x and y.
common_mistakes: Writing 'hence proved' without naming the principle.
steps.memory_tip: Name the principle in one sentence — it is worth a full mark.
